You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos and their word order); quote only ASKED_BY words, never DEFERRALS or
    CONTEXT, which are not requirements;
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
Each quote may carry a CONTEXT line: where it was said and what it answered (the message it
replied to, a link it pasted, the list it approved). Use CONTEXT only to resolve what the
quote's own words point at: "#1", "this", "it", "all your recommendations". Never cut a
requirement from CONTEXT alone, and never quote it; every quote comes from the person's words.
  - "shouldnt #1 be automated?" with CONTEXT saying #1 was "catch up the archive" is the
    requirement "#1 automated", read as the archive catching up by itself.
  - A quote that only approves or accepts what someone proposed ("i approve all your
    recommendations", "yes do that") is not a requirement for an approval. When CONTEXT lists
    what was approved, cut one requirement per approved item, each quoting the approving
    words; when it does not, cut it once as kind "process".
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.
When the user message lists REQUIREMENTS ALREADY CUT, skip Step 1: those are the requirements, fixed.
Do not split, rename, renumber or re-quote them; answer only with one mapping per listed id, using
those ids.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
criterion covers it.

Step 3. If a requirement is covered by no criterion, check DEFERRALS. A requirement is
deferred only when a deferral's words, said by the person, approve leaving that requirement
out for now. Give the deferral's number, or 0 when none applies. Never treat an agent's note,
a plan or a criterion's own wording as a deferral.

Step 4. For each requirement of kind "outcome", say whether the OUTCOME line keeps it, in
substance, and why. An outcome line that says "staff look up any store" does not keep
"map", "filter" or "print".

Be strict and literal. Judge only from the text given.

OUTCOME (the agent's one-line restatement):
<<<Worlds stay faithful as they grow too big for an AI to track: the engine works out every knock-on effect and blocker of an attempt, however long the chain (100 links, 50 at once), and delivers those results to an AI judge with the blockers: first the facts and nearby checks it can work out with no rule, then the full test run of the rule the judge proposes, before anything is installed; the judge decides only what no rule covers, its rulings become checked rules for everyone (installed during the run by default, or held with the attempt pending for my approval by the world's setting), the person being bribed decides whether a bribe works, saved runs replay unchanged, and a mechanism, who holds its credential and the norm about who should use it stay separate, as in Ostrom's grammar, so a password learned by social engineering works for whoever holds it while the breach of 'only Alice should log in' is recorded, and a world can stop at a stopping point written in plain words that the judge assesses after each round, alongside its round and spending limits.>>>

CRITERIA:

[A1] 
  criterion: Facts have their implications and blockers worked out automatically: any change of a fact sets off every knock-on effect it implies, and any step a fact blocks is shown with that blocker, however long the chain; Brian's 50 chains of 100 links finish in the same moment, every step names the step that caused it, and a loop still stops.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open the saved run "fifty chains" (50 chains of 100 steps set off in one moment): https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=NQ0Slg2LMrms (2) Read the moment's summary line, then open any three steps and follow each to the step that caused it. (3) Open the saved run "loop" and read the same moment's summary line and steps: https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=gv6uHVQMYRr1 (4) Open the saved run "truck without fuel" and read step 40 and what comes after it: https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=Um6gKNtlkIiE 
  expected: "fifty chains": the summary line reads "5,000 steps run, 5,000 with a cause, no refusal", and each opened step leads to the step that caused it. "loop": each rule fires once for each thing and the moment ends. "truck without fuel": after step 40 comes item 41 in orange, "blocked: truck leaves (truck) did not happen: “the truck has fuel” was not true (it was 0). Nothing followed from it.", and no step follows it.

[A2] 
  criterion: When someone tries something no rule covers, the judge is handed what the engine can already work out, including the blockers installed rules already name, and, before anything is installed, the net changes, every blocker, the chain's length and where it stopped for the rule it proposes (the run page and run record keep every step of a long chain); the judge is the world's own game master, not a prompt of ours.
  demonstration: (1) Open the live run https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=P0ds3rwI2r9a (a fresh run of the port world: the description "A small port: Rosa, the customs officer, signs inspection releases. Vik, a trader, has 40 coins and a crate he has not declared." with hand-written rules; a fresh build, which writes its rules afresh, need not reproduce the strings below). (2) On the run page, open "Every attempt" and click Vik's offer of 40 coins to Rosa (round 1, the dashed square). (3) Read, in order: what the judge was given first (facts and blockers), the rule it proposed, the test run of that rule, and the judge's answer to it. (4) Open the judge panel and read who ruled and what the judge read. (5) Open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=cYXKe6reqpwn (blocked chain ruling), where the rule the judge proposes would set off a chain that reaches a truck with no fuel; click the round 1 attempt and read the test run and what the judge read before it answered. (6) Open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=j-Rpi_CO1V_j (long line ruling), where the rule the judge proposes sets off 5,000 steps; click the round 2 attempt, read what the judge read (the net changes and blockers) and then the run page's list of all 5,000 steps. 
  expected: Port: first given, the facts (Vik holds 40 coins; Rosa and Vik are at the customs desk) and, under Rosa's moves, the blocker an installed rule already names ("sign release: blocked, inspected is false"). Proposed: a rule that lets coins change hands between people at the same place (in the link above "hand coins", Vik's own move; in the earlier saved run the judge wrote it as Rosa's move, "accept coin offer", Vik the payer; either wording is the same rule). Test run: coins move to Rosa, Vik's purse empties, nothing else follows, no blocker. The judge confirms. The judge panel says the ruling came from the world's game master, and the facts, the blocker and the test run all appear in what the judge read. "blocked chain ruling": the test run shows "blocked at step 40: the truck has no fuel" and the chain stopping there, and that blocker appears in what the judge read before it confirmed, revised or withdrew. "long line ruling": the judge read the net changes (grouped, with their count of 5,001), no blocker, chain length 5,000 and stopped as settled, and the run page lists all 5,000 steps.

[A3] 
  criterion: The judge only decides what no rule covers: an attempt an installed rule covers is decided by that rule, and if one of its checks fails the attempt is refused with the blocker named and the judge is not asked.
  demonstration: (1) Open the live run https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=ZrR5GbzE9SZg (empty purse: the coin rule is already installed and Ines, a trader with no coins, hands Rosa coins; she is briefed to bluff, and no resident did it unprompted in 7 runs). (2) On the run page, open "Every attempt" and click the trader's offer. 
  expected: The offer reads "Refused, because this check was false: the giver holds that many coins" (the rule's own check), nothing changes, and the row says "Decided by rule, judge not asked."

[A4] 
  criterion: A judge ruling becomes a rule that passed the rules check and test run and then decides the same attempt for everyone; a ruling the rule language cannot express is refused and listed as a gap; and the one thing Brian asked to make configurable, whether a checked ruling made during a run is installed at once (default, 'Approved by Create') or held with the attempt pending until he approves ('Wait for my approval'), is a per-world setting, with every ruling listed on the run page either way.
  demonstration: (1) Default (Approved by Create): open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=3hWjWii4Q3BQ (the port world, two traders). Open "Rulings in this run". (2) Wait for my approval, held: open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=qlKA3Wp9v3kp (rounds 1 and 2 only). Open the ruling list. (3) Approve: open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=F_ND9bo29lvp (the same two rounds, then the owner's Approve sent with round 3). Open the ruling list and the round lines. (4) Reject: open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=iKefhnd6zOkc (the same two rounds, then Reject). Open the ruling list and round 4. (5) Price times quantity: open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=MrEqGi3Z40Kf (the lumberyard world) and its ruling list. 
  expected: Default: R1 hand-over-coins reads "installed, passed the rules check and test run"; Ines's round 2 attempt "went to the person whose choice it is"; in round 3 Ines's and Vik's handovers read "decided by rule, judge not asked (allowed)". Held: R1 accept-coin-handover is held and Ines's attempt is pending; nothing changed. Approve: R1 reads installed, "The owner approved it"; Ines's waiting try went to Rosa and Rosa's acceptance is decided by rule. Reject: R1 rejected; Ines's waiting try and her round 4 try are refused naming R1; no coins move. Price times quantity: planned as a language gap; live, the judge wrote a fixed-number rule instead (see status).

[A5] 
  criterion: A voluntary exchange settles only after the named people choose its exact terms, once, under the current world constraints; installing or approving a rule cannot supply consent or revive an expired offer.
  demonstration: (1) Open the planned repaired port exchange demonstration. Select Vik's offer, read its id, giver, named respondent, exact amount/conditions, terms hash and expiry, then follow the delivered observation to Rosa's own acceptance or refusal. (2) Compare acceptance of an unconditional coin offer with an offer explicitly conditional on a signed release. In both, open the signature action's actual feasibility result separately from Rosa's willingness to accept. (3) Open both saved regression cases: the giver-shaped rule from install-default and the receiver-shaped rule from wait-approve. Follow the repaired versions: an unaccepted giver move cannot settle, and Ines cannot take Vik's coins without Vik's offer to her. (4) Open the altered-terms cases: the wrong respondent, substituted giver, changed amount or changed terms hash attempts to accept. Inspect each refusal and unchanged asset balances. Include an attempted direct submission, not just an absent menu item. (5) Open the Wait for my approval cases. Compare approval of an unaccepted offer, timely approval of accepted_pending_rule, and approval after the offer expires or is withdrawn. Inspect the rule fingerprint attached to the pending offer. (6) Open a case where the held rule is revised to different effects and a case where it is rejected. Read why the old offer cannot settle and its terminal state. (7) Open a case accepted by both people but infeasible at settlement because resources, location or another blocker changed. Inspect the failed settlement, unchanged balances and terminal failed state. (8) Open a successful settlement, then its duplicate acceptance/submission in the same branch. Compare the one settlement event id, consumed offer and asset balances; replay the recorded branch and inspect its recorded offer lifecycle. (9) Open expiry/withdrawal cases and the final run record at a budget or round stop. Confirm pending offers and terminal dispositions are visible; distinguish replay/fork of an old snapshot from a second settlement in the current branch. 
  expected: The proposer assents to immutable terms through the specific offer; only its named respondent can accept or reject it. Acceptance of coins is not itself a signature: an unconditional transfer may settle while a later signature is refused; if signing is an explicit settlement condition, the entire bargain must be expressible and feasible atomically or be refused as a blocker/language gap. Both giver- and receiver-shaped voluntary rules use the same guard. Wrong parties, altered terms, missing/expired/withdrawn offers and duplicate acceptances cannot settle. Timely accepted_pending_rule settles only after exact-rule approval and fresh feasibility checks; approval alone supplies no consent, revised effects require a new offer/response, and rejected rules terminate pending offers. Success publishes one atomic asset change with consumed offer/event id; infeasibility publishes no asset change and terminal failed state. Recorded replay preserves these decisions without model calls or invented consent. Historical runs without offer records retain their old semantics and do not certify the repaired contract.

[A6] 
  criterion: What a mechanism checks, who holds a credential and who is supposed to use it are kept apart, following Ostrom's grammar of institutions: a barcode gate opens for any valid code while 'only signed cargo should pass' is a norm, a password can be phished and then works for whoever holds it, breaking a norm has consequences only when someone notices and acts, and each norm and rule is written in the grammar's parts (who it applies to; must, must not or may; what; when; and, for a rule, what happens otherwise and who enforces it), so a norm without an 'otherwise' reads differently from an enforced rule.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open the saved run "password". (2) Follow Mallory's phishing message to Alice, Alice's reply, and Mallory's login; read what the run page says about the norm and what happened after it. (3) Open the port run J4 saves (the port description "A small port: Rosa, the customs officer, signs inspection releases. Vik, a trader, has 40 coins and a crate he has not declared." with the same fixture rules as the J2 port run) where Rosa signs Vik's release for a bribe; read what opened the gate and what the page says about the cargo norm. (4) Open the world's norms list and read each norm. 
  expected: After the phishing, Mallory holds Alice's password; the computer logs Mallory in; the page shows "norm broken: only Alice should log in"; a consequence follows only after someone who saw it acts. In the port, the gate opens because it read a valid code, not because of who holds it, and the cargo norm's breach is shown separately. Each entry in the norms list reads as: who it applies to; must, must not or may; what; when; and, where there is one, what happens otherwise and who enforces it. "Bribery is forbidden, or else the inspector fines you" shows an otherwise and an enforcer; "only Alice should log in" shows none and is marked a norm.

[A7] 
  criterion: Saved runs replay unchanged after the knock-on limit is removed: each run records the limit it ran under and replay uses it, while new runs have no such limit.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open a run saved before the limit was removed that stopped at the old limit, and replay it: https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=OWjUKGkZzOtr (the wind-chain world, 40 dominoes, saved on build 43663e9 before J0). (2) Run the same world again as a new run and open the same moment: https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=f-Eyu2sx7-q_ (the same world run under J0). 
  expected: The replay matches the saved run step for step and shows "refused: knock-on effects did not settle within 32 steps (the limit this run ran under)". The new run of the same world has no such refusal, and its summary line counts every step.

[A8] 
  criterion: A world stops by its budget, by a number of rounds, or at a stopping point written in plain words that the judge assesses after each round: each is an optional condition of the world's stop setting, beside quiet rounds, and the run stops at whichever fires first and says which.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder Create page, open Options and under When to stop a run tick "Stop when this run has spent $" and enter 0.05; build a world (its people are played by AI, so its rounds have a recorded cost; a free scripted run records $0 and never reaches a spending limit) and press Play until it stops. (2) Build a world again with "Stop after 3 rounds" ticked; press Play until it stops. (3) Build a team world from the description "A small team of three, Ana, Ben and Cai, must agree a budget for the quarter; each can propose an amount and each can accept or counter", with "Stop when" set to "stop once the team has agreed a budget"; run it until it stops, then open the stop line, the judge's reason and one earlier round's panel. (4) Build that team world again with "Stop after 3 rounds" as well, where the team cannot agree by round 3; run it. 
  expected: Budget: the run stops after the round in which its recorded AI spending reached $0.05 and says "Stopped at round N: this run had spent $X of its $0.05 limit" (with "it went a little over" when the last round took it past). Rounds: it stops at round 3 with "the limit of 3 rounds you set". Stopping point: the run stops after the round in which the team agrees a budget and says "Stopped at round N: the team has agreed a budget (the judge's reading of your stopping point)"; the reason opens to what the judge read, and each earlier round's panel shows "stopping point: not yet" with the judge's reason. With the round limit of 3 as well, the run stops at round 3 on the round limit instead.

You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos and their word order); quote only ASKED_BY words, never DEFERRALS or
    CONTEXT, which are not requirements;
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
Each quote may carry a CONTEXT line: where it was said and what it answered (the message it
replied to, a link it pasted, the list it approved). Use CONTEXT only to resolve what the
quote's own words point at: "#1", "this", "it", "all your recommendations". Never cut a
requirement from CONTEXT alone, and never quote it; every quote comes from the person's words.
  - "shouldnt #1 be automated?" with CONTEXT saying #1 was "catch up the archive" is the
    requirement "#1 automated", read as the archive catching up by itself.
  - A quote that only approves or accepts what someone proposed ("i approve all your
    recommendations", "yes do that") is not a requirement for an approval. When CONTEXT lists
    what was approved, cut one requirement per approved item, each quoting the approving
    words; when it does not, cut it once as kind "process".
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.
When the user message lists REQUIREMENTS ALREADY CUT, skip Step 1: those are the requirements, fixed.
Do not split, rename, renumber or re-quote them; answer only with one mapping per listed id, using
those ids.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
criterion covers it.

Step 3. If a requirement is covered by no criterion, check DEFERRALS. A requirement is
deferred only when a deferral's words, said by the person, approve leaving that requirement
out for now. Give the deferral's number, or 0 when none applies. Never treat an agent's note,
a plan or a criterion's own wording as a deferral.

Step 4. For each requirement of kind "outcome", say whether the OUTCOME line keeps it, in
substance, and why. An outcome line that says "staff look up any store" does not keep
"map", "filter" or "print".

Be strict and literal. Judge only from the text given.

You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos and their word order); quote only ASKED_BY words, never DEFERRALS or
    CONTEXT, which are not requirements;
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
Each quote may carry a CONTEXT line: where it was said and what it answered (the message it
replied to, a link it pasted, the list it approved). Use CONTEXT only to resolve what the
quote's own words point at: "#1", "this", "it", "all your recommendations". Never cut a
requirement from CONTEXT alone, and never quote it; every quote comes from the person's words.
  - "shouldnt #1 be automated?" with CONTEXT saying #1 was "catch up the archive" is the
    requirement "#1 automated", read as the archive catching up by itself.
  - A quote that only approves or accepts what someone proposed ("i approve all your
    recommendations", "yes do that") is not a requirement for an approval. When CONTEXT lists
    what was approved, cut one requirement per approved item, each quoting the approving
    words; when it does not, cut it once as kind "process".
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.
When the user message lists REQUIREMENTS ALREADY CUT, skip Step 1: those are the requirements, fixed.
Do not split, rename, renumber or re-quote them; answer only with one mapping per listed id, using
those ids.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
criterion covers it.

Step 3. If a requirement is covered by no criterion, check DEFERRALS. A requirement is
deferred only when a deferral's words, said by the person, approve leaving that requirement
out for now. Give the deferral's number, or 0 when none applies. Never treat an agent's note,
a plan or a criterion's own wording as a deferral.

Step 4. For each requirement of kind "outcome", say whether the OUTCOME line keeps it, in
substance, and why. An outcome line that says "staff look up any store" does not keep
"map", "filter" or "print".

Test run: coins move to Rosa, Vik's purse empties, nothing else follows, no blocker. The judge confirms. The judge panel says the ruling came from the world's game master, and the facts, the blocker and the test run all appear in what the judge read. "blocked chain ruling": the test run shows "blocked at step 40: the truck has no fuel" and the chain stopping there, and that blocker appears in what the judge read before it confirmed, revised or withdrew.   demonstration: (1) Open the live run https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=ZrR5GbzE9SZg (empty purse: the coin rule is already installed and Ines, a trader with no coins, hands Rosa coins; she is briefed to bluff, and no resident did it unprompted in 7 runs).   expected: The offer reads "Refused, because this check was false: the giver holds that many coins" (the rule's own check), nothing changes, and the row says "Decided by rule, judge not asked."

  criterion: A judge ruling becomes a rule that passed the rules check and test run and then decides the same attempt for everyone; a ruling the rule language cannot express is refused and listed as a gap; and the one thing Brian asked to make configurable, whether a checked ruling made during a run is installed at once (default, 'Approved by Create') or held with the attempt pending until he approves ('Wait for my approval'), is a per-world setting, with every ruling listed on the run page either way.

(2) Wait for my approval, held: open https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=qlKA3Wp9v3kp (rounds 1 and 2 only). Open the ruling list.   criterion: A voluntary exchange settles only after the named people choose its exact terms, once, under the current world constraints; installing or approving a rule cannot supply consent or revive an expired offer.
  demonstration: (1) Open the planned repaired port exchange demonstration. Select Vik's offer, read its id, giver, named respondent, exact amount/conditions, terms hash and expiry, then follow the delivered observation to Rosa's own acceptance or refusal. In both, open the signature action's actual feasibility result separately from Rosa's willingness to accept. Include an attempted direct submission, not just an absent menu item. (5) Open the Wait for my approval cases. Compare approval of an unaccepted offer, timely approval of accepted_pending_rule, and approval after the offer expires or is withdrawn. Inspect the rule fingerprint attached to the pending offer. Inspect the failed settlement, unchanged balances and terminal failed state. (8) Open a successful settlement, then its duplicate acceptance/submission in the same branch. Compare the one settlement event id, consumed offer and asset balances; replay the recorded branch and inspect its recorded offer lifecycle.   expected: The proposer assents to immutable terms through the specific offer; only its named respondent can accept or reject it.   criterion: What a mechanism checks, who holds a credential and who is supposed to use it are kept apart, following Ostrom's grammar of institutions: a barcode gate opens for any valid code while 'only signed cargo should pass' is a norm, a password can be phished and then works for whoever holds it, breaking a norm has consequences only when someone notices and acts, and each norm and rule is written in the grammar's parts (who it applies to; must, must not or may; what; when; and, for a rule, what happens otherwise and who enforces it), so a norm without an 'otherwise' reads differently from an enforced rule.

  criterion: Saved runs replay unchanged after the knock-on limit is removed: each run records the limit it ran under and replay uses it, while new runs have no such limit.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open a run saved before the limit was removed that stopped at the old limit, and replay it: https://brianmills.dev/world-builder/?run=OWjUKGkZzOtr (the wind-chain world, 40 dominoes, saved on build 43663e9 before J0).   criterion: A world stops by its budget, by a number of rounds, or at a stopping point written in plain words that the judge assesses after each round: each is an optional condition of the world's stop setting, beside quiet rounds, and the run stops at whichever fires first and says which.

(3) Build a team world from the description "A small team of three, Ana, Ben and Cai, must agree a budget for the quarter; each can propose an amount and each can accept or counter", with "Stop when" set to "stop once the team has agreed a budget"; run it until it stops, then open the stop line, the judge's reason and one earlier round's panel. You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos and their word order); quote only ASKED_BY words, never DEFERRALS or
    CONTEXT, which are not requirements;
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
Each quote may carry a CONTEXT line: where it was said and what it answered (the message it
replied to, a link it pasted, the list it approved). Use CONTEXT only to resolve what the
quote's own words point at: "#1", "this", "it", "all your recommendations". Never cut a
requirement from CONTEXT alone, and never quote it; every quote comes from the person's words.
  - "shouldnt #1 be automated?" with CONTEXT saying #1 was "catch up the archive" is the
    requirement "#1 automated", read as the archive catching up by itself.
  - A quote that only approves or accepts what someone proposed ("i approve all your
    recommendations", "yes do that") is not a requirement for an approval. When CONTEXT lists
    what was approved, cut one requirement per approved item, each quoting the approving
    words; when it does not, cut it once as kind "process".
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.
When the user message lists REQUIREMENTS ALREADY CUT, skip Step 1: those are the requirements, fixed.
Do not split, rename, renumber or re-quote them; answer only with one mapping per listed id, using
those ids.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
